en: The Scripture on the Heart-Mantra Spoken by the Buddha, in one fascicle, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Yuezhi people during the Western Jin Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was dwelling at Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha, together with five hundred bhikṣus.
The Buddha was accompanied by his fourfold assembly.

At dawn, the Buddha donned his robes, took up his alms bowl, and went to a certain district to wander for alms. Various devas, nāgas, and spirits followed behind him in attendance. Upon arriving at the gate of a brahmin’s residence, he stood there; the Buddha then emitted a great light that universally illuminated the ten directions.

At that time, the brahmin’s wife was tending the hearth and cooking rice when she saw the light shining upon her body. Her body attained tranquility and she experienced immeasurable joy; she thought to herself:
"This radiant splendor is not like that of the sun, moon, Śakra, Brahmā, the Four Heavenly Kings, or the various devas; I am personally overwhelmed by such blissful joy."

Looking back, he beheld the Buddha, upright and exceptionally beautiful, like the moon among the stars, with sublime marks towering high and all secondary characteristics complete; his faculties were serene, free from decline, established in the supreme tranquility, and attained the foremost concentration. He was like the sun first appearing upon a mountain ridge, or like a Wheel-Turning King visiting his great palace, attended by ministers and followers;

or like Śakra manifesting his presence in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, or like the Brahmā King in the seventh station; or like the snow upon a high mountain, brilliantly radiant and universally visible. His joy redoubled as he reflected again:
"Now that I have been able to behold the Buddha and his disciples, my long-cherished vow is truly fulfilled; I wish to offer this food to the Perfectly Awakened One."

Reflecting inwardly, I see that this foolish man does not believe in the Way and its Virtue; his mind is set upon heterodox doubts and the sixty-two views. Seeing what my wife has bestowed, he will surely give rise to resentment and enmity.

Due to the transgressions of past lives, he has lost his heroic and valiant son; now, as a captive woman bound by others, I wish to bestow [this child] upon the Holy Honored One, yet I cannot do so of my own accord. I ought to protect my intention—what should I do?
He immediately scraped up some rice and took a ladleful of broth to offer to the Buddha.
By the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, a hundred-flavored meal appeared spontaneously within the bowl. At that time, the Buddha gave a blessing, pronouncing this verse of praise:
“Even if one were to provide a hundred horses, With saddles and bridles adorned with gold and silver,”
To bestow gifts upon others is not as good as a ladleful of rice gruel;
even if one were to provide a chariot made of the seven treasures, filled to the brim with all manner of rare gems,
the merit of offering that ladleful of rice gruel to the Buddha exceeds that of the former.
If one were to give a hundred white elephants adorned with bright pearls and necklaces,
yet offer but a single ladle of broth to the Buddha, that merit would surpass the former;
it is like the holy Wheel-Turning King or the noble Queen Prabhāvatī.
Of peerless beauty and symmetry, with bodies adorned by necklaces of the seven jewels—
of such wondrous types as these, a hundred each,
all bestowed as gifts upon others, it would not equal even a single ladle of broth.
At that time, the brahmin remained in quietude and listened; hearing the Buddha’s praise, his mind was filled with doubt, and he stepped forward to ask the Buddha:
"What is the value of a single ladle of rice broth, such that you should offer such high praise?"

To give various treasures, elephants, horses, and carriages—which are beyond reproach—and yet claim they are not equal to the gift of a ladle of rice gruel; though this rice gruel is not worth a single coin, one instead praises it with billions of times more admiration—who would believe such a thing?
Thereupon, the World-Honored One immediately manifested his broad and long tongue, covering his face and extending upward as far as the Brahma Heaven. He addressed the brahmin, saying:

"For countless hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas, I have constantly practiced the six perfections of sincerity, bestowing all forms of peace and security upon others without begrudging anything I possessed; it is through this that I have obtained such a tongue. How could one possibly attain it through false speech?"
"I wish to ask you something; please answer with complete sincerity.
Have you ever traveled back and forth between Śrāvastī and Rājagṛha? Along the way, there is a tree named Nyagrodha; does its shade provide shelter for five hundred chariots?"
He replied, “Indeed, there is such a tree; it is what I have seen.
The World-Honored One asked again:
“How large is that child?
He replied, “In form,
it is like a mustard seed.”
The Buddha told the brahmin:
"You are truly a double-tongued man.
If it were truly the size of a mustard seed, how could the tree be so massive?"
He replied, "Truly so; I dare not deceive you.
The Buddha spoke again, saying:

"If a seed the size of a mustard grain can grow into a vast tree, such that the earth's capacity for growth is insufficient to contain it and its canopy spreads ever wider—how much more so must this be true for the Tathāgata, the Unsurpassed, the Truly Realized, the Perfectly Awakened One, who is the universal victor through the convergence of immeasurable merit?"

The matters of precept, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation; great kindness and vast compassion that rescue all without exception; and the merit and blessings of making offerings with such a feast are beyond calculation.
The brahmin remained silent, unable to offer any reply.

At that moment, the Buddha smiled, and light of five colors issued from his mouth, illuminating the ten directions and the beings of the five destinies: the desires of the devas were stilled, the hearts of humans rejoiced, the hungry ghosts were satiated, the pains of those in hell ceased, and the minds of animals were opened. Their karmic offenses were eliminated, and they followed the light to come before the Buddha.
The manner in which all Buddhas manifest a smile always possesses a fixed omen:
when bestowing the prediction of enlightenment upon a Bodhisattva, light shines throughout the ten directions and enters through the crown of the head;
when bestowing the prediction upon a Pratyekabuddha, the light enters through the mouth.
When bestowing the prediction of enlightenment upon a śrāvaka, the light enters the shoulder;
when speaking of rebirth in the heavens, the light enters the navel;
when speaking of descending among humans, the light enters the knee.
It is said that the three types of suffering enter from the soles of the feet to the heart.

The joy of the Buddhas does not smile out of desire, nor out of anger, nor out of delusion; it does not smile out of negligence, nor for the sake of sensual gain, nor for honor and nobility, nor for wealth and abundance. Now, the Buddha universally and equally pities all sentient beings; he practices the smile of great compassion, which is free from these seven [motives].

The worthy Ānanda distinguished seven dharmas—knowledge of the Dharma, understanding of its meaning, awareness of the proper time, comprehension of the seasons, mastery of the affairs of the assembly, self-examination of one’s own person, and clarity regarding the faculties of others—and immediately rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and asked the Buddha:
“For what reason does the Buddha smile?”
"I pray that you will explain its meaning.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Did you see the brahmin’s wife give rise to this great resolve?"
He replied, “I have seen it.
The Buddha said:

"When this woman reaches the end of her life, she shall transform from her female form to become a man; she will be born among the gods as the most honored among them, and descending again to the world, she will be the highest among men. She will understand the profound and wondrous Dharma as being like an illusion or a transformation, like the moon, a shadow, an echo, or a mirage in the water. After thirty kalpas, she shall attain Buddhahood, named Citta-prakāśa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān."
The brahmin’s heart was subdued; prostrating himself with his five limbs touching the ground, he reproached himself with all his heart and confessed, saying:

“I am like a small child, foolish and shrouded in darkness; harboring doubts and hesitations, I failed to recognize the Great Sage and uttered coarse words from my mouth. I pray only that you forgive these transgressions.”
The Buddha said: "Excellent! Excellent!"

If one recognizes one's own faults, takes refuge in the Buddha, and repents of one's calamities and defilements within the Path, Dharma, and Vinaya, then those transgressions will diminish, and merit will increase day by day.
The brahmin stepped forward and petitioned:
"May you deign to show great compassion!
Grant us your grace and protection, allowing us to go forth into the homeless life."
The Buddha immediately accepted him as a śramaṇa; his hair and beard fell away, and the dharma-robe appeared upon his body.
At that time, the World-Honored One preached the Four Noble Truths—suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path—and the brahmin leaped for joy, his outflows exhausted and his mind liberated.

When the Buddha had spoken thus, the venerable Ānanda, the fourfold assembly, and the devas, humans, nāgas, and spirits all resolved their minds upon the Way; filled with joy, they bowed their heads in prostration.
The Sūtra on the Heart-Mantra Spoken by the Buddha
